Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 82, drawn from the sources found and read:

---

## Psalm 82 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Background / Title

**"A Psalm of Asaph."** Asaph was the great singer and musician of David and Solomon's era, also regarded as a prophet in his musical compositions (1 Chronicles 25:1; 2 Chronicles 29:30). Gill suggests Asaph wrote under a spirit of prophecy, with respect to the times of Christ when corruption among Jewish rulers — both civil and ecclesiastical — was great. Kimchi thought it was written about the time of Jehoshaphat, who appointed new judges after earlier ones had become corrupt (2 Chronicles 19:5). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott notes the psalm represents the deep Hebrew conviction that "Justice is the fundamental virtue of society, and that its corruption implies total disorganisation and ruin." God is presented with calm dignity as presiding Judge among the magistrates themselves. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

---

### v. 1 — "God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods"

**Traditional reading (human judges):** The "gods" (Hebrew *elohim*) are human judges and magistrates who act as God's delegates and representatives on earth. As Morgan put it: "They are called *elohim*, because they are His delegates; they administer His will; they are His executive agents." God stands in their midst as the ultimate Judge, observing and holding them accountable. Martin Luther noted that this verse both establishes the authority of princes (God appoints them and calls them "gods") and limits it (they are accountable to Him). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

Ellicott says "Standeth" (a participle) has an official ring — God has taken His official place as president of the bench of judges. He translates "congregation of the mighty" as "assembly of God" — a divine assembly, elsewhere "the congregation of Jehovah" referring to Israel in its religious character. He sees the "gods" as men delegated with office from God, citing Exodus 21:6 and possibly Exodus 22:8–9. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

Gill, while noting some take it as angels (Syriac version, Aben Ezra), concludes civil magistrates are meant — those called *elohim* in Exodus 21:6. He stresses that Christ, the Son of God, judges among them: "to whom all judgment is committed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

A different view: The Pulpit Commentary interprets "congregation of the mighty" as the Divine assembly in *heaven* (citing Job 1:6; 2:1; Isaiah 6:1–2). It argues that *El* (singular) "can scarcely mean the 'mighty ones of earth,'" so God holds court in heaven surrounded by divine ministers who execute His behests. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

**Piper / Reformed (angelic beings view):** John Piper reads the "gods" as angelic beings — what the New Testament calls "principalities and powers and world rulers of this present darkness." God comes to the assembly of these "gods" and rebukes them for the pattern of evil in the world. This interprets the scene as operating on two levels: one seen (human), one unseen (angelic). (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/putting-the-gods-in-their-place)

**NET Bible / modern scholarship:** The NET Bible translates "assembly of El" and notes three possibilities: (1) God presiding over His own heavenly assembly; (2) *El* as a superlative ("the great assembly"); (3) a reference to the Canaanite high god El, making the psalm a bold polemic against Canaanite religion — Israel's God invades El's assembly, denounces its gods, and announces their demise. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=82)

**Bible.org (Bob Utley):** Summarises five interpretive options: Israeli judges, pagan judges/kings, pagan gods, national angels (cf. Deuteronomy 32:8; Daniel 10:13), or angels of the heavenly council. He leans toward national angels, arguing that Psalm 82:7 ("you will die like men") demands the addressees are *not* human. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-82)

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Reads it as Jehovah watching over His vice-gerent rulers in Israel, holding them accountable for just judgment. Only among God's appointed administrators were judges called *Elohim* — "to whom the law came" (John 10:34–35). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-82.html)

---

### v. 2 — "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah"

These are God's own words confronting the unjust judges. Gill writes: "These are the words not of the psalmist, but of the divine Person that stands in the congregation of the mighty … calling the unjust judges to an account." He notes this is "very applicable to the rulers and judges of the Jewish nation in the times of Christ." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott calls "How long?" a "terrible severity in this Divine *Quousque tandem!*" and notes the phrase "judge unjustly" is literally "judge iniquity." "Accept the persons" (literally "lift up the faces") arises from the Eastern custom of prostration before a judge — the accepted suitor is permitted to rise, so it means showing favouritism. Leviticus 19:15, which forbids exactly this, is "evidently in the poet's mind." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary calls it "the cry of the impatient Jehovah" (Cheyne). Accepting persons — favouring people because of their position or outward circumstances — was strictly forbidden in the Mosaic Law (Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:19; Leviticus 19:15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes: "God did not do it to compliment them or pay them honor. He did it to confront them." Spurgeon is quoted: "Our village squires and country magistrates would do well to remember this." The *Selah* gives "the offenders pause for consideration and confession." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

---

### v. 3 — "Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed."

God commands the judges to do their duty. Gill explains "defend" is literally "judge them" — take up their cause, give them a hearing, do not deny them justice because they lack money or friends. Judges are to imitate God, "who is the Father of the fatherless, the Judge of the widows" (Psalm 10:14). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott notes this verse "recalls the solemn curse in Deuteronomy 27:19" (cursed is he who perverts justice due the fatherless). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary says these commands are "covert reproaches" — by telling them what they ought to do, God rebukes them for what they have failed to do. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

Enduring Word quotes Adam Clarke: "You [judges] are their natural protectors under God. They are oppressed: punish their oppressors, however rich or powerful." Martin Luther is also cited: "These … three verses, indeed the whole psalm, every prince should have painted on the wall of his chamber." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

---

### v. 4 — "Rescue the weak and needy; save them from the hand of the wicked."

This verse intensifies the command: not merely to judge fairly, but actively to deliver. The Pulpit Commentary notes the poor were "terribly oppressed" and needed rescue, citing Job 29:12, Isaiah 1:17, and Micah 3:2–3. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

Gill observes that this parallels the widow in Jesus' parable who pleaded with the unjust judge for deliverance from her adversary (Luke 18:3). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Enduring Word notes: "Law has too often been an instrument for vengeance in the hand of unscrupulous men … It is for the judge to prevent such villainy" (Spurgeon). Also cited is King Jehoshaphat's charge in 2 Chronicles 19:6–7 as a parallel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

---

### v. 5 — "They do not know or understand; they wander in the darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken."

**Who is "they"?** The traditional reading applies this to the unjust judges themselves. Enduring Word (following Boice) summarises three perils that doom governments forgetting God: ignorance ("they do not know"), inept action ("they walk about in darkness"), and societal collapse ("all the foundations of the earth are unstable"). Spurgeon adds: "When peasants may be horsewhipped by farmers with impunity, and a pretty bird is thought more precious than poor men, the foundations of the earth are indeed sinking." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

Gill calls their ignorance "wilful and affected" — they shut their eyes against light and evidence. When justice is perverted, "towns, cities, commonwealths, kingdoms, and states, are thrown into the utmost disorder and confusion." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott pictures a pause — "that interval between warning and judgment which is God's pity and man's opportunity" — but the expostulation "falls dead without a response." The men are "infatuated by their position and blinded by their pride." He translates "they walk on in darkness" as "they *let themselves* walk in darkness," the Hebrew conjugation implying that will, not circumstance, causes this blindness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary differs slightly: it takes this not as an aside from the Judge but as a complaint by Jehovah addressed to the angelic host present (v. 1). It too stresses the ignorance is "not accidental and excusable … but wilful and guilty." The foundations shaken are "the fundamental bases on which the life of man upon the earth rests, the very principles of morality." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

**Piper / Reformed (angelic view):** In this reading, the "they" refers to the angelic "gods" — principalities and powers who, behind human authorities, promote injustice. The shaking of earth's foundations reflects cosmic disorder caused by rebellious spiritual powers. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/putting-the-gods-in-their-place)

**Bible.org (Utley):** Argues that vv. 5–8 "cannot refer to humans but must refer to angels," listing as evidence: the cosmic language of "all the foundations of the earth are shaken," the title "sons of the Most High," and the pronouncement "you will die like men" (implying they are not men). (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-82)

---

### v. 6 — "I have said, 'You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.'"

This is the most debated verse in the psalm, famously quoted by Jesus in John 10:34–36.

**Traditional (human judges) reading:** All sources taking this view agree: God gave human judges the title "gods" (*elohim*) because of their office as His representatives. The Pulpit Commentary explains: "in my Law I have called you gods" (see Exodus 21:6; 22:8–9), since they judge on God's behalf. They possess "not therefore 'gods' in the strictest sense, but … a derived, and so a qualified, divinity." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

Gill: "I have said" refers to the Law (Exodus 21:6) — they were constituted judges by His appointment. "Children of the Most High" because of "their eminency and dignity, their high office, post, and place." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott catches the drama: "Again the Divine voice breaks the silence with an emphatic *I*. 'From me comes your office and your honoured title, gods; now from me hear your doom.'" He adds the intriguing note that Constantine quoted vv. 1 and 6 at the opening of the Council of Nicaea, "to remind the bishops that their high office should raise them above jealousy and party feeling." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

Enduring Word notes that Exodus 21:6 and 22:8–9 use the same Hebrew word *elohim*, translated "judges." Jesus' argument in John 10 was: "If God gave these unjust judges the title 'gods' because of their office, why do you consider it blasphemy that I call Myself the 'Son of God'?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

**Piper / Reformed (angelic reading):** John Piper explicitly rejects the human-judges reading. He argues the "gods" are angelic beings — "sons of the Most High" parallels "sons of God" in Job 1:6 and 38:7. He says Jesus, in John 10, was *not* teaching that humans are called gods; rather, Jesus used Psalm 82 as "a shrewd escape maneuver" — if Scripture calls lesser beings (angels) "gods" and "sons of God" without blasphemy, how much less blasphemous is it for Jesus, consecrated and sent by the Father, to call Himself "Son of God"? Piper insists Jesus "doesn't equate himself with those gods in Psalm 82." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/putting-the-gods-in-their-place; https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/did-jesus-say-we-are-gods)

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Takes the human-judge view: "God's princes and judges were called 'gods', Elohim, meaning representatives of God, in their appointed offices in Israel to administer His laws equitably, with dignity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-82.html)

---

### v. 7 — "But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall."

All commentators agree this pronounces death and judgment on those addressed. The irony is sharp: those called "gods" will die like ordinary men.

Enduring Word: "They were like gods only in a symbolic sense; they themselves would die like men and face judgment before the Judge of all the earth." Poole is cited: "like men; or, like ordinary men, as the Hebrew word *adam* sometimes signifies." Trapp adds darkly: "Our Henry VIII was told on his death bed that he should go to the place of princes; which was no great comfort, if the old proverb be true, that hell is paved with the crowns of princes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

Gill: "The wise man dies as the fool, the king as the peasant … death levels and makes all alike." He notes a possible double meaning — not only physical death but eternal death ("dying in their sins," John 8:21). As for "fall like one of the princes," he suggests this may refer to Satan who "fell like lightning from heaven" (Luke 10:18), or the giants of the flood, or heathen tyrants, or the fall of the Jewish nation itself (Romans 11:11). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott renders the end of the verse: "yea, altogether will ye princes perish" (literally "like one man"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: "The name of 'gods,' even the fact of your being representatives of God, shall not save you from condign punishment." It sees "fall like one of the princes" as coming to an untimely end as so many princes in Israel's history had done (Joshua 12:9–24; various judges). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

**For the angelic view:** This verse is a key argument. Bible.org (Utley) argues that saying "you shall die like men" to beings who are *already* men makes little sense — it strongly implies the addressees are *not* human. Piper likewise says: "They are not men but they will die like men." The "gods" (angelic powers) will perish as ignominiously as the human sinners they have used. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-82; https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/putting-the-gods-in-their-place)

---

### v. 8 — "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance."

The psalmist now speaks in his own voice, calling on God to take up the judgment that earthly judges have failed to execute.

Enduring Word: This is a plea for God to take His place as ultimate Judge. Human judges failed; Asaph asks God to take judgment into His own hands. "You shall inherit all nations" points ultimately to Jesus Christ. Clarke is quoted: "It is only by the universal spread of Christianity over the world, that the reign of righteousness and justice is to be established: and of whom can it be said that he shall inherit all nations, but of Jesus Christ?" Spurgeon adds: "The last days shall see him enthroned … The second advent is still earth's brightest hope." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-82/)

Gill reads "Arise, O God" as the words of the prophet or church addressing Christ, who is God over all. Universal justice will not take place "till that time comes" when Christ inherits all nations. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/82.htm)

Ellicott sees the poet taking "a wider sweep of view" that includes not only administrators of law but the political situation of the nation. "It is as if, despairing of the amendment of the corrupt magistrates, the poet … takes his case out of their hands … and entrusts it to the Great Judge of the world, to whom, as a special inheritance, Israel belonged, but who was also to show His claim to the submission and obedience of all nations." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/82.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: God is asked to judge not only Israel but "the whole world," since "God is the King of all the earth" (Psalm 47:2). The word "inherit" (or "dost inherit") means all nations are His possession. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/82.htm)

---

## Major Interpretive Divide: Who Are the "Gods"?

The single biggest disagreement among Protestant traditions and scholars concerns the identity of the *elohim* ("gods") in vv. 1 and 6. Three main views appear in the sources:

| View | Who are the "gods"? | Key proponents in sources |
|------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| **Human judges** | Earthly magistrates/rulers acting as God's representatives. Jesus' use in John 10:34 is taken as confirming this. | Enduring Word / David Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic), John Gill (Baptist), Ellicott (Anglican), Pulpit Commentary, Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, Spurgeon |
| **Angelic beings** | The "divine council" — angelic powers, "sons of God," principalities behind earthly rule. They are NOT human, hence "you shall die *like men*." | John Piper / Desiring God (Reformed Baptist), Bob Utley / Bible.org (evangelical) |
| **Pagan gods (polemic)** | The psalm invades the Canaanite pantheon, denouncing its gods as failed and doomed. A bold polemic against Canaanite religion. | NET Bible notes, Willem VanGemeren (cited in NET) |

The Pulpit Commentary occupies an interesting middle ground: it reads the "congregation" as a heavenly assembly of divine ministers (angels), yet interprets the rebuke as ultimately directed at earthly judges who are called "gods" by delegation. It does not choose one side exclusively.

**Note on Catholic and Orthodox sources:** The search limit was reached before sites such as newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org could be searched. These readings could not be included.

**Note on Word of Faith / prosperity teaching:** The well-known Word of Faith use of Psalm 82:6 ("ye are gods") to teach that believers are "little gods" was not found in any of the approved sites, which uniformly reject that interpretation. GotQuestions.org addresses it indirectly by noting that *elohim* can refer to judges, angels, or pagan deities — not to believers as divine beings. The excerpt available states: "The Hebrew word *elohim* is also translated 'judges' in Exodus 21:6 and 22:8, 9, and 28." (https://www.gotquestions.org/you-are-gods.html)
